full_text_en:
China Construction Bank Corporation, Huaihua Branch v. China Huarong Asset Management Co., Ltd., Hunan Branch, et al. — dispute over execution objection by a third party

[Ruling Summary]

1. Cases of execution objection lawsuits may be reviewed and handled by reference to the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Handling of Execution Objection and Reconsideration Cases by People's Courts, while at the same time, a substantive examination must be conducted, based on the specific circumstances of the case, as to whether the third party enjoys civil rights and interests sufficient to preclude compulsory execution.

2. The question of whether a non-consumer purchaser of real property can preclude the enforcement application of a mortgagee may be determined by conducting a substantive examination of the rights of both parties based on factors such as the nature of the rights, the sequence of when the rights were obtained, whether there was fault in obtaining the rights, and how to reduce or prevent the recurrence of risks, in light of the specific facts of the case.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2022) Supreme People's Court Final No. 34

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): China Construction Bank Corporation, Huaihua Branch. Domicile: No. 380 Yingfeng Middle Road, Hecheng District, Huaihua City, Hunan Province.

Responsible Person: Wu Shuhua, Branch Manager.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): China Huarong Asset Management Co., Ltd., Hunan Branch. Domicile: No. 976 Wuyi Avenue, Kaifu District, Changsha City, Hunan Province.

Responsible Person: Long Zhilin, General Manager of the Branch.

Third Party at First Instance: Hunan Chenxi Huazhong Cement Co., Ltd. Domicile: Huomachong Industrial Park, Chenxi County, Hunan Province.

Third Party at First Instance: Xie Yongjian, male, born on November 16, 1964, Han ethnicity, residing at No. 329 Yingfeng Middle Road, Hecheng District, Huaihua City, Hunan Province.

Agent ad litem: Pu Yafei, resident of Yinwan Community, Yingfeng Street Office, Hecheng District, Huaihua City, Hunan Province.

Third Party at First Instance: Chen Taofang, female, born on April 5, 1968, Han ethnicity, residing at No. 78 Haoting West Road, Qifu New Village, Shiguang Road, Panyu District, Guangzhou City, Guangdong Province.

Agent ad litem: Pu Yafei, resident of Yinwan Community, Yingfeng Street Office, Hecheng District, Huaihua City, Hunan Province.

The appellant, China Construction Bank Corporation, Huaihua Branch (hereinafter referred to as CCB Huaihua Branch), in a dispute over execution objection by a third party against the respondent, China Huarong Asset Management Co., Ltd., Hunan Branch (hereinafter referred to as Huarong Hunan Branch), and the third parties at first instance, Huaihua Yingtai Construction Investment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yingtai Company), Dongxing Construction Engineering Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Dongxing Company), Hunan Chenxi Huazhong Cement Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huazhong Company), Xie Yongjian, and Chen Taofang, being dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2020) Xiang Min Chu No. 1 of the Hunan High People's Court, filed an appeal to this Court. After the case was docketed on February 8, 2022, this Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing. The agents ad litem of the appellant CCB Huaihua Branch, Jiang Tiehua and Lei Shaohua, the agents ad litem of the respondent Huarong Hunan Branch, Zhou Daoming and Li Kangyu, the common agent ad litem of the third parties at first instance Yingtai Company, Dongxing Company, and Huazhong Company, Deng Shuimiao, and the common agent ad litem of the third parties at first instance Xie Yongjian and Chen Taofang, Pu Yafei, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The case is now concluded.

CCB Huaihua Branch's grounds for appeal: 1. Reverse the judgment of the first instance; 2. Order that the property located at No. 1-16, Building 2, Phase II of Yingtai International, Yingfeng West Road, Hecheng District, Huaihua City, Hunan Province (hereinafter referred to as the property in question) shall not be subject to execution; 3. Confirm that the priority right of Huarong Hunan Branch to receive satisfaction from the property in question shall not be opposable against CCB Huaihua Branch; 4. The litigation costs of the first and second instances shall be borne by Huarong Hunan Branch. Facts and reasons: (1) Article 28 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Handling of Execution Objection and Reconsideration Cases by People's Courts (hereinafter referred to as the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration) and Article 17 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on the Seizure, Freeze, and Auction of Property in Civil Enforcement by People's Courts (hereinafter referred to as the Provisions on Seizure, Freeze, and Auction) (2005 version) are applicable to cases where the applicant for enforcement has a security interest in the subject matter of enforcement and should serve as the basis for adjudicating this case. 1. Articles 28 through 30 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration constitute the exception provided in Article 27, which states: "If the applicant for enforcement has a security interest or other priority right in the subject matter of enforcement that is opposable against the third party, the people's court shall not uphold the third party's objection to exclude execution, unless otherwise provided by law or judicial interpretation." 2. Articles 28 through 30 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration in fact protect the buyer's right of expectation of property rights. The purpose of these three judicial interpretations is to address the issue of priority protection for those who, under special circumstances, have not yet obtained property rights but hold a specific claim to the property. 3. The understanding and application of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration also clarify in the interpretation of Article 27 that the phrase "unless otherwise provided by law or judicial interpretation" in that article includes Articles 28 through 30 of the same judicial interpretation. 4. The Supreme People's Court's civil ruling (2018) Supreme People's Court Min Shen No. 4090 also determines that Articles 28 and 29 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration are exceptions to Article 27, and that a buyer's right of expectation of property rights that meets the conditions of Articles 28 and 29 can preclude the compulsory enforcement of an applicant for enforcement who enjoys a security interest or other priority right. In accordance with the principle of consistent adjudication for similar cases, this precedent should be referenced in adjudicating this case. (2) The facts regarding CCB Huaihua Branch's purchase and possession of the property in question fully satisfy the provisions of Article 28 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration, which states: "In the enforcement of monetary claims, if a buyer raises an objection to real property registered under the name of the person subject to enforcement, and if the following conditions are met and the buyer's rights can preclude execution, the people's court shall uphold the objection: (1) a legally valid written purchase contract has been signed before the people's court's seizure; (2) the real property has been legally possessed before the people's court's seizure; (3) the full purchase price has been paid, or a portion of the purchase price has been paid in accordance with the contract and the remaining price is delivered for execution as required by the people's court; (4) the failure to register the transfer is not attributable to the buyer's own fault." These facts also satisfy the provisions of Article 17 of the Provisions on Seizure, Freeze, and Auction (2005 version), which states: "If the person subject to enforcement sells property requiring registration for transfer to a third party, and the third party has paid part or all of the purchase price and has actually possessed the property but has not yet completed the registration procedures for the transfer of title, the people's court may seize, freeze, or auction the property; if the third party has paid the full purchase price and has actually possessed the property but has not completed the registration procedures, and if the third party is not at fault in this regard, the people's court shall not seize, freeze, or auction the property." CCB Huaihua Branch has no fault whatsoever regarding the failure to transfer the registration or to register a caution for the property in question. 1. CCB Huaihua Branch signed a legally valid written purchase contract before the mortgage and the people's court's seizure. The Commercial Housing Purchase Contract between CCB Huaihua Branch and Yingtai Company for the property in question was signed on January 31, 2013, while Huarong Hunan Branch registered the mortgage on May 27, 2013, and the people's court seized the property in question on September 29, 2014. 2. CCB Huaihua Branch legally possessed the real property before the mortgage and the people's court's seizure. According to the terms of the Commercial Housing Purchase Contract, Yingtai Company was required to deliver the property in question to CCB Huaihua Branch by March 29, 2013. After taking possession of the property in March 2013, CCB Huaihua Branch renovated it in August 2013 and has continuously used it to the present. CCB Huaihua Branch's possession of the property also predates the time when Huarong Hunan Branch registered the mortgage and applied for seizure. 3. CCB Huaihua Branch has paid the full purchase price, or has paid a portion of the purchase price in accordance with the contract and is willing to deliver the remaining price for execution as required by the people's court. By March 28, 2013, CCB Huaihua Branch had already paid 95% of the purchase price, i.e., RMB 16,163,110; by November 27, 2013, the payment had reached 98%. Before the mortgage and seizure, CCB Huaihua Branch had almost paid the full purchase price. CCB Huaihua Branch is also willing to deliver the remaining price for execution as required by the court. 4. The failure to register the transfer or to register a caution is not attributable to CCB Huaihua Branch's own cause. (1) The failure to register the transfer of the property in question is due to reasons related to the property itself and the seller, and CCB Huaihua Branch has no fault in this regard. At the time of the sale, the property was off-plan and the title certificate could not be obtained. Moreover, due to reasons attributable to the seller Yingtai Company (including issues of mortgage and seizure), the title certificate still cannot be obtained to this day. Therefore, the failure to complete the registration procedures for the transfer of the property is not due to any cause on the part of CCB Huaihua Branch, and CCB Huaihua Branch has no fault in this regard. (2) According to the agreement, the obligation to register a caution for the Commercial Housing Purchase Contract was on the seller Yingtai Company, not on CCB Huaihua Branch. Furthermore, the seller Yingtai Company mortgaged the property in question to Huarong Hunan Branch within a very short period, which CCB Huaihua Branch could not avoid. The failure to register a caution is not attributable to CCB Huaihua Branch, and the seller's breach of contract in failing to register a caution should not be imputed to CCB Huaihua Branch. (3) Finding that CCB Huaihua Branch was at fault for the failure to register the transfer or the caution in this case would be inconsistent with the relevant judicial spirit of the Supreme People's Court. CCB Huaihua Branch took proactive steps to request registration from the seller and had sufficient objective reasons for the failure to register a caution. Pursuant to Article 127 of the Minutes of the National Conference on Civil and Commercial Trial (2019), CCB Huaihua Branch should not be found at fault. (4) After purchasing the property, CCB Huaihua Branch paid the deed tax and fulfilled various preconditions necessary for registering a caution. Moreover, the Commercial Housing Purchase Contract signed between CCB Huaihua Branch and the seller Yingtai Company was a standard formal contract for commercial housing, jointly supervised by the Huaihua Administration for Industry and Commerce and the Huaihua Real Estate Administration, with a red hard cover. These circumstances were sufficient to give CCB Huaihua Branch a reasonable expectation that the purchase was legally valid. (3) Before Huarong Hunan Branch registered the mortgage over the property in question and before the court seized it, CCB Huaihua Branch had already legally possessed the property. CCB Huaihua Branch's legal possession of the property based on the legally valid Commercial Housing Purchase Contract is also a right protected by law. By analogy with the principles of priority protection for possession acquired through a prior lease under the former Property Law of the PRC and other relevant laws and regulations, possession arising from a sale relationship, which has a stronger property-right attribute than a lease, should be even more entitled to priority protection under the law. If a lessee's possession of a house, obtained based on a valid lease established prior to the mortgage or seizure, is protected by law in priority over the mortgagee or the seizing creditor, even if the property is disposed of, the lessee's legal possession should be protected. In summary, whether from a legal or common-sense perspective, CCB Huaihua Branch's rights in the property in question should take precedence over Huarong Hunan Branch's mortgage rights and are sufficient to preclude Huarong Hunan Branch's enforcement of the property.

Huarong Hunan Branch argued in defense: (1) CCB Huaihua Branch's argument that its civil rights in the property in question satisfy the conditions for a general real property buyer to preclude execution under Article 28 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration is not legally sound and cannot be established. The focal issue of legal application in this case is whether a general real property buyer who meets the conditions of Article 28 can preclude enforcement by an applicant for enforcement who is a mortgagee. CCB Huaihua Branch's assertion that it has the right to preclude execution reflects a misunderstanding of the law. 1. Based on an understanding of Article 27 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration, a general real property buyer under Article 28 does not fall within the exception "unless otherwise provided by law or judicial interpretation" in Article 27. That is, where the applicant for enforcement holds a mortgage over the subject matter of enforcement, Article 28 has no application. Whether the third party meets the four conditions of Article 28 is not a dispositive fact for adjudication; regardless of whether such conditions are met, the mortgagee's enforcement of the mortgaged property cannot be precluded. 2. Precedent judgments of the Supreme People's Court hold that a general buyer cannot oppose the enforcement of a mortgagee (see the Search Report for Similar Cases). 3. From academic interpretations by Supreme People's Court judges, it is generally accepted that a general real property buyer cannot oppose a mortgagee. (2) Even if Article 28 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration were considered an exception to Article 27, CCB Huaihua Branch does not meet the conditions for applying Article 28. 1. CCB Huaihua Branch's possession of the property in question is not legal possession. The date of registration of the mortgage by Huarong Hunan Branch was May 27, 2013. Both the Mortgage Agreement between Huarong Hunan Branch and Yingtai Company and the Certificate of Mortgage Right issued by the registration authority recorded the mortgaged property as a construction in progress. A "construction in progress" means a building that has not yet completed the final acceptance inspection and is still under construction and installation. Moreover, to this day, the mortgaged property has not completed final acceptance inspection and remains a construction in progress. Article 61, paragraph 2 of the Construction Law of the PRC provides: "A construction project may be delivered for use only after it has passed the final acceptance inspection; if it has not passed the inspection or has failed the inspection, it shall not be delivered for use." Under this prohibitive provision of law, Yingtai Company's delivery of a construction in progress to CCB Huaihua Branch, and CCB Huaihua Branch's possession and use of a construction in progress that has not passed final acceptance inspection, are both illegal. Therefore, this case does not satisfy the condition in Article 28(2) of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration that "the real property has been legally possessed before the people's court's seizure." 2. CCB Huaihua Branch does not satisfy the condition in Article 28(4) of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration that "the failure to register the transfer is not attributable to the buyer's own cause." In multiple judgments, the Supreme People's Court has pointed out that to meet this condition, there must be circumstances such as "the buyer and seller have jointly submitted an application for ownership transfer registration to the real estate registration authority and the authority has accepted it, or the buyer has initiated a lawsuit or applied for arbitration in a dispute with the seller over the ownership transfer registration, or there are other reasonable objective reasons." However, in this case, CCB Huaihua Branch has provided no evidence that it jointly applied for transfer registration with Yingtai Company to the real estate registration authority. Although the Commercial Housing Purchase Contract between CCB Huaihua Branch and Yingtai Company stipulated that "within 30 days after delivery, the materials for registration of ownership shall be submitted to the property registration authority for filing," in fact, Yingtai Company did not file the purchase contract, and CCB Huaihua Branch did not urge Yingtai Company to file the contract or register a caution. In fact, if the Commercial Housing Purchase Contract had been filed, the relevant registration authority would have, under the Urban Real Estate Administration Law of the PRC and the Measures for the Administration of Pre-sale of Commercial Housing by Cities, placed the transacted property under a restricted rights status, making it impossible for Yingtai Company to mortgage the property. Furthermore, on May 27, 2013, Huarong Hunan Branch obtained the mortgage over the property in question. After that date, CCB Huaihua Branch paid the final installment of the purchase price to Yingtai Company on November 27, 2013, and signed a property management contract with the property management company on November 18, 2013, thereby actually possessing the property. It can be seen that during the transaction process, CCB Huaihua Branch still had the opportunity to discover the fact that the property had been mortgaged and to take timely remedial measures, but it missed this opportunity due to negligence. From the above facts, it can be seen that CCB Huaihua Branch did not pay sufficient attention to the legality, compliance, and safety of the purchase transaction. The failure to register the transfer of the property and its subsequent mortgage are related to CCB Huaihua Branch's own negligence. Therefore, CCB Huaihua Branch's possession of the property is not in good faith, and the failure to register the transfer is attributable to its own cause. 3. CCB Huaihua Branch's citation of the former Property Law of the PRC and the Provisions on Seizure, Freeze, and Auction is clearly irrelevant to this dispute. CCB Huaihua Branch's opinion on the procedural aspects of this case also contradicts the effective judgments of the Supreme People's Court, and Huarong Hunan Branch need not respond to that. In summary, whether under legal provisions, legal principles, or the principle of consistent adjudication for similar cases, CCB Huaihua Branch's reliance on Article 28 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration to block the realization of Huarong Hunan Branch's mortgage right is unfounded, and CCB Huaihua Branch has also failed to meet the application conditions set forth in Article 28. Therefore, its grounds for appeal are contrary to law and cannot be established. Huarong Hunan Branch requests that CCB Huaihua Branch's appeal be dismissed and the original judgment be upheld.

CCB Huaihua Branch's claims at the first instance were: 1. Order that the property in question shall not be subject to execution; 2. Confirm that the priority right of Huarong Hunan Branch to receive satisfaction from the property in question shall not be opposable against CCB Huaihua Branch.

The court of first instance found the following facts: On January 31, 2013, Yingtai Company signed a Commercial Housing Sale and Purchase Contract with the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank, stipulating that Yingtai Company would sell the property in question to the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank; the commercial premises had an area of 438.5 square meters, a unit price of RMB 38,800 per square meter, a total sale price of RMB 17,013,800, and related taxes and fees of RMB 1,055,891; Yingtai Company was to deliver the premises to the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank by March 29, 2013, and within 30 days after delivery, submit the documents for ownership registration to the property registration authority for record; Yingtai Company undertook to complete the property ownership certificate within two years after the delivery of the property. After the contract was signed, on December 31, 2009, March 28, 2013, and November 27, 2013, the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank remitted a deposit and purchase price of RMB 1,000,000, RMB 15,163,110.64, and RMB 500,000 respectively to the designated account of Yingtai Company, and paid the corresponding deed tax for the property purchase. On November 18, 2013, the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank signed the Yingtai International Property Management Contract with Huaihua Yingtai Mall Management Co., Ltd. On December 2, 2013, the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank paid RMB 23,679 in property management fees to Huaihua Yingtai Mall Management Co., Ltd.

On May 23, 2013, the Huarong Hunan Branch entered into a Mortgage Agreement (No. Hunan Y1830015-6) with Yingtai Company, stipulating that Yingtai Company would provide mortgage security for its debts owed to the Huarong Hunan Branch using its unsold commercial properties under construction and their apportioned land within the Yingtai International Project Phase II located at Yingfeng West Road, Hecheng District, Huaihua City. On May 27, 2013, the Huarong Hunan Branch and Yingtai Company registered a mortgage on the property in question, which was a construction in progress, with the Huaihua Municipal Housing Authority.

On September 19, 2014, the court of first instance accepted the case of the Huarong Hunan Branch v. Yingtai Company, Dongxing Company, Huazhong Company, Xie Yongjian, and Chen Taofang regarding a contract dispute. On September 29, 2014, the court of first instance issued a civil ruling (2014) Xiang Gao Fa Min Er Chu Zi No. 32-1, sealing up the property in question under the name of Yingtai Company. On December 12, 2014, the court of first instance issued a civil judgment (2014) Xiang Gao Fa Min Er Chu Zi No. 32, ruling to rescind the Debt Restructuring Agreement between the Huarong Hunan Branch and Yingtai Company, ordering Yingtai Company to repay the Huarong Hunan Branch RMB 98,000,000 in debt, plus restructuring gains, liquidated damages, and attorney's fees of RMB 695,431, and ordering Dongxing Company, Huazhong Company, Xie Yongjian, and Chen Taofang to bear joint and several liability. It was further ordered that if the debt was not repaid when due, the Huarong Hunan Branch had the right to have the mortgaged properties of Yingtai Company (3,194.53 square meters and 2,709.09 square meters, and the corresponding land use rights, with housing mortgage certificate numbers: Huai Fang He Ta Zi No. 513003032 and Huai Fang Jian He Cheng Zi No. 313000033) converted into money by discounting or auctioning or selling the mortgaged properties and to receive priority in satisfaction of its claim. Neither party appealed, and the judgment became effective. Yingtai Company failed to perform the repayment obligations determined by the civil judgment (2014) Xiang Gao Fa Min Er Chu Zi No. 32 when due, and the Huarong Hunan Branch applied to the court of first instance for compulsory enforcement. After accepting the enforcement case, the court of first instance issued a public auction announcement (2015) Xiang Gao Fa Zhi Zi No. 22 on August 21, 2017, intending to auction multiple properties under the name of Yingtai International, including the property in question, as determined by the civil judgment (2014) Xiang Gao Fa Min Er Chu Zi No. 32. The Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank objected and submitted an enforcement objection to the court of first instance. On December 12, 2017, the court of first instance issued a civil ruling (2017) Xiang Zhi Yi No. 75, rejecting the objection request of the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank. The Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank then filed this lawsuit.

The court of first instance also found that the Huaihua Intermediate People's Court of Hunan Province, on June 5, 2018, issued a civil ruling (2018) Xiang 12 Po Shen No. 1, accepting Yingtai Company's application for reorganization; on August 29, 2018, issued civil rulings (2018) Xiang 12 Po Shen No. 6 and No. 7, accepting the reorganization applications of Dongxing Company and Huazhong Company; and on November 16, 2019, issued a civil ruling (2018) Xiang 12 Zhi No. 204-1, ruling to suspend the enforcement of items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of the civil judgment (2014) Xiang Gao Fa Min Er Chu Zi No. 32, on the ground that Yingtai Company, Dongxing Company, and Huazhong Company had entered into bankruptcy reorganization proceedings.

The court of first instance held that, taking into account the submissions of all parties, the issues in dispute in this case were: (1) whether the present action for execution objection should continue to be heard after the third party entered into bankruptcy proceedings; and (2) whether the civil rights enjoyed by the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank over the property in question could preclude compulsory enforcement by the people's court.

(1) On issue one. The Huarong Hunan Branch argued that, under Article 19 of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the People's Republic of China, because the judgment debtor, Yingtai Company, and others had entered into bankruptcy reorganization proceedings, the enforcement proceedings in this case had already been suspended by the people's court's ruling, and the prerequisite for the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank to initiate the lawsuit was not established, so the claim should be dismissed. The court of first instance held that, although an action for execution objection arises from enforcement proceedings, it is essentially an independent trial proceeding with its own specific procedural and substantive functions. First, procedurally. This case is an action for execution objection by a person not involved in the execution, initiated by the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank, seeking to preclude the people's court from enforcing the property in question. When a people's court considers whether to accept such a lawsuit, it should examine whether the conditions for filing an action for execution objection by a person not involved in the execution, as provided in Article 119 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (as amended in 2017) and Article 305 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (effective 2015), are satisfied. Upon examination, the Huarong Hunan Branch applied for compulsory enforcement of the property under the name of Yingtai Company based on the mortgage right confirmed by the effective judgment. After its objection was rejected, the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank, as a person not involved in the execution, filed an action for execution objection before the court of first instance. This complies with the provisions of the above laws and judicial interpretations and should be accepted in accordance with the law. At the same time, during the period when this action for execution objection was initiated, the judgment debtors, Yingtai Company, Dongxing Company, and Huazhong Company, entered into bankruptcy reorganization proceedings. According to Article 20 of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the People's Republic of China, "After the people's court accepts a bankruptcy application, any civil litigation or arbitration concerning the debtor that has commenced but has not yet concluded shall be suspended; such litigation or arbitration shall continue after the administrator takes over the debtor's property." During the trial of this case, the people's court that accepted the bankruptcy reorganization applications of Yingtai Company, Dongxing Company, and Huazhong Company had already appointed their administrators, who could represent the judgment debtors in continuing to participate in the litigation. Therefore, it was procedurally proper for this case to continue to be heard. Second, substantively. First, functionally, an action for execution objection, as a remedy targeting enforcement proceedings, not only serves the function of precluding compulsory enforcement by the court but also has the function of confirming the priority order of substantive rights. In this case, although the judgment debtors had entered into bankruptcy reorganization proceedings, whether the bankrupt enterprise ultimately undergoes reorganization or liquidation, neither can replace the substantive function of the action for execution objection in confirming the priority of a creditor's rights. Second, in terms of effect, if the property in question is unsealed due to bankruptcy, the property will be taken over by the judgment debtor's bankruptcy administrator; if it is unsealed due to a successful action for execution objection, the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank could demand continued performance of the contract. Although both involve the same measure of lifting the sealing, the suspension of enforcement due to the judgment debtor's entry into bankruptcy proceedings differs in legal basis from the cessation of enforcement due to the exclusion of the court's enforcement measures through an action for execution objection. The two procedures have different bases and bring about different legal effects and impacts on the rights and interests of the parties. Therefore, the hearing of the action for execution objection should not be stopped merely because the judgment debtor entered into bankruptcy proceedings, resulting in a suspension of enforcement. In summary, the Huarong Hunan Branch's argument lacked legal basis, and the action for execution objection should continue to be heard after the judgment debtor entered into bankruptcy proceedings in this case.

(2) On issue two. In this case, the Huarong Hunan Branch applied to the people's court for compulsory enforcement based on the mortgage right confirmed by the civil judgment (2014) Xiang Gao Fa Min Er Chu Zi No. 32. The Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank, relying on the civil rights arising from its execution of the Commercial Housing Sale and Purchase Contract with Yingtai Company, payment of the purchase price, and possession and use of the property, claimed to preclude the compulsory enforcement by the people's court. Therefore, whether the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank could preclude enforcement depended on whether its civil rights over the property in question had priority over the mortgage right of the Huarong Hunan Branch. The Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank alleged that, before the property in question was sealed up by the people's court, it had entered into a legally valid Commercial Housing Sale and Purchase Contract with Yingtai Company, paid most of the purchase price, and actually possessed the property. According to Article 17 of the Provisions on Sealing, Seizure, and Freezing of Property in Civil Enforcement (effective 2005) and Article 28 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration, it enjoyed civil rights sufficient to preclude compulsory enforcement by the people's court. The court of first instance held: First, the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank had not yet fully paid the purchase price for the property in question, and after signing the Commercial Housing Sale and Purchase Contract with Yingtai Company, it neither promptly registered the contract for record nor publicly disclosed that the property had been purchased by it in accordance with the law. At the same time, the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank also failed to submit evidence that it had promptly urged Yingtai Company to go through the transfer registration procedures. Therefore, it was at fault for the failure to register the transfer of the property in question. Consequently, the property in question did not meet the conditions under Article 17 of the Provisions on Sealing, Seizure, and Freezing of Property in Civil Enforcement (effective 2005) under which a people's court must not seal, seize, or freeze the property. This claim of the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank could not be established and was not supported. Second, Article 27 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration provides that, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or judicial interpretation, a person not involved in the execution shall not preclude compulsory enforcement by a application enforcement creditor based on a security interest or other priority right. Article 28 provides that, in the enforcement of monetary claims, a general purchaser of a property may, when certain conditions are met, preclude compulsory enforcement by the people's court. Since this case involves the issue of priority between a mortgage right and other rights, the provisions of Article 27 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration should be applied by analogy. However, the above provisions do not specify whether the exceptions provided by law or judicial interpretation include other provisions of this interpretation. Therefore, when determining exceptions to Article 27, it is inappropriate to directly apply other provisions of the same interpretation, including Article 28. The court of first instance held that Article 1 of the former Reply of the Supreme People's Court on the Priority of Compensation for Construction Project Price stipulates: "When adjudicating real estate dispute cases and handling enforcement cases, the people's courts shall, in accordance with Article 286 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, determine that the priority right of a construction project's contractor takes precedence over mortgage rights and other claims." Article 2 stipulates: "Where a consumer has paid all or most of the purchase price for a commercial property, the contractor's priority claim for the project price with respect to that commercial property shall not prevail against the buyer." According to the above provisions, the right of a consumer of commercial property who has paid all or most of the purchase price takes precedence over the mortgage right of the mortgagee. However, this special provision only applies to consumers of commercial property who purchase housing for residential purposes and have paid all or most of the purchase price; ordinary purchasers under a housing sale and purchase contract are not covered by the above provision. In this case, the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank purchased the property in question for use as a bank business outlet, not for residential purposes. Therefore, according to the provisions of the above judicial interpretation, the civil rights enjoyed by the Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank over the property in question do not fall within the statutory exception under Article 27 of the Provisions on Execution Objection and Reconsideration that may take precedence over a mortgage right and cannot take precedence over the mortgage right that has been registered and confirmed by an effective judgment in favor of the Huarong Hunan Branch. The Huaihua Branch of China Construction Bank may assert its relevant civil rights in the bankruptcy proceedings in accordance with the law.

This Court holds that, based on the parties' arguments, the issues in dispute in this second-instance trial are: whether China Construction Bank Huaihua Branch has civil rights and interests in the property involved sufficient to exclude compulsory enforcement.

(I) Regarding the application of law in this case

An action of opposition to enforcement originates from an outsider's objection to enforcement. It is a remedy proceeding initiated when an outsider files an objection to the subject matter of enforcement and is either rejected or upheld by the enforcement court, and the outsider or the applying enforcement party is dissatisfied with the ruling. Thus, there is a certain correlation and commonality between the enforcement objection and the action of opposition to enforcement, but they belong to different procedural stages with different functional orientations and different principles and standards for reviewing the civil rights and interests of outsiders. The enforcement objection, as part of the enforcement procedure, focuses on a formal review of rights over the subject matter of enforcement. Its institutional function is to swiftly and uninterruptedly realize the creditor's rights determined by the effective judgment, valuing procedural efficiency while balancing substantive fairness. In contrast, the action of opposition to enforcement, as a subsequent litigation procedure connected to the enforcement objection, is an independent, complete substantive trial procedure. Its value orientation prioritizes fairness over efficiency, determining the ownership of the subject matter of enforcement through substantive review, and then deciding whether the outsider's civil rights and interests are sufficient to exclude compulsory enforcement, thereby achieving substantive relief for the civil rights of the outsider or the applying enforcement party. The "Provisions on Enforcement Objection and Review" are judicial interpretations governing "enforcement objection and review cases" in enforcement proceedings and should, in principle, apply only to enforcement proceedings. However, given the correlation and commonality between actions of opposition to enforcement and enforcement proceedings, prior to the issuance of specific laws or judicial interpretations on the review standards for actions of opposition to enforcement, such cases may refer to the relevant provisions of the "Provisions on Enforcement Objection and Review" to review and determine whether the outsider's civil rights and interests are sufficient to exclude compulsory enforcement. However, if there is significant theoretical and practical controversy over whether certain provisions of the "Provisions on Enforcement Objection and Review" apply to the dispute involved, and the parties also have substantial disagreements and respective justifications on this issue, then it is inappropriate to refer to the relevant provisions of this judicial interpretation. Instead, the court should return to the essence of the action of opposition to enforcement, conduct a substantive review of whether the outsider has civil rights and interests sufficient to exclude compulsory enforcement based on the specific circumstances of the case, and, in accordance with Article 310, paragraph 1 of the "Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China," which provides: "For an action of opposition to enforcement brought by an outsider, the people's court shall, after trial, handle it as follows according to the circumstances: (1) if the outsider has civil rights and interests in the subject matter of enforcement sufficient to exclude compulsory enforcement, the court shall rule that the subject matter of enforcement shall not be enforced; (2) if the outsider does not have civil rights and interests in the subject matter of enforcement sufficient to exclude compulsory enforcement, the court shall dismiss the claim," the court shall decide whether to uphold the outsider's objection.

In this case, referring to Article 27 of the "Provisions on Enforcement Objection and Review," which provides: "If the applying enforcement party has, according to law, a security interest or other priority right over the subject matter of enforcement that is effective against the outsider, the people's court shall not uphold the outsider's objection to exclude enforcement, unless otherwise provided by law or judicial interpretation," the general principle is that when a mortgagee and a purchaser come into conflict, the mortgage should be given priority protection, unless otherwise provided by law or judicial interpretation. The former "Reply of the Supreme People's Court on Issues Concerning the Priority of the Construction Project Price Claim" provided that after a consumer pays all or most of the purchase price for a commercial housing unit, the rights and interests in the purchased unit can be asserted against the priority of the construction project price claim and the mortgage, to protect the consumer's right to survival. However, since China Construction Bank Huaihua Branch is not a consumer of commercial housing (the purchased property is for business use), it does not enjoy the special protection rights that commercial housing consumers have based on the right to survival. China Construction Bank Huaihua Branch argues that the proviso of Article 27 of the "Provisions on Enforcement Objection and Review" includes Article 28 of the same judicial interpretation, which provides that an ordinary real estate buyer's (non-consumer) right to expect property rights may exclude enforcement. It claims that this case should be reviewed under Article 28. In contrast, Huairong Hunan Branch insists that the proviso of Article 27 does not include Article 28, and thus there is no room for applying Article 28. Each party submitted corresponding authorities and similar cases. Since the law and judicial interpretations do not clearly stipulate this issue, the first-instance judgment held that it was inappropriate to directly apply other provisions, including Article 28, which has some basis. However, the first-instance judgment failed to conduct a substantive comparison of the civil rights enjoyed by the outsider objector and the applying enforcement party in light of the specific characteristics of an action of opposition to enforcement and make a corresponding determination. Instead, it merely relied on the former "Reply on the Priority of Construction Project Price Claim" to find that China Construction Bank Huaihua Branch was not a commercial housing consumer and dismissed its objection. This application of law had certain flaws, and this Court corrects it.

As for China Construction Bank Huaihua Branch's argument that Article 17 of the "Provisions on Seizure, Detention, and Freezing in Civil Enforcement" (effective 2005) should be the basis for adjudicating this case, the "Provisions on Seizure, Detention, and Freezing in Civil Enforcement" are judicial interpretations formulated to "further standardize the measures of seizure, detention, and freezing in civil enforcement." Article 17 provides: "If the person subject to enforcement sells property that requires transfer registration to a third party, and the third party has paid part or all of the purchase price and actually occupies the property, but has not yet completed the registration of transfer of title, the people's court may seize, detain, or freeze the property; if the third party has paid the full purchase price and actually occupies the property, but has not completed the registration of transfer, and if the third party is not at fault for this failure, the people's court shall not seize, detain, or freeze the property." This provision is a procedural rule on whether property that a third party has paid for and actually occupies but has not registered title transfer may be seized, detained, or frozen. It does not involve a substantive comparison of rights between the applying enforcement party and the third party who purchased the property, nor does it address whether the third party's civil rights and interests can exclude compulsory enforcement. Therefore, it is not automatically applicable in actions of opposition to enforcement.

(II) Regarding whether the civil rights and interests of China Construction Bank Huaihua Branch in the property involved are sufficient to exclude compulsory enforcement

In this case, to determine whether the civil rights and interests of China Construction Bank Huaihua Branch in the property involved are sufficient to exclude the compulsory enforcement applied for by Huairong Hunan Branch, the court may conduct a substantive review of the rights of both parties based on the nature of the rights, the time sequence of acquiring the rights, whether there was fault in acquiring the rights, and how to reduce or prevent the recurrence of risk, in conjunction with the specific facts of the case, and then compare which party's rights have superior standing and should be given priority protection, and make a corresponding determination.

1. In terms of the nature of the rights: China Construction Bank Huaihua Branch has a right to expect property rights in the property involved, while Huairong Hunan Branch has a mortgage. Both have priority over ordinary creditor's rights.

Expectant right of property, as a right state transitioning from creditor's right and being in the preparatory stage of acquiring property, is characterized by actual possession and has attributes that distinguish it from ordinary creditor's rights and resemble property rights. In this case, CCB Huaihua City Branch, based on the Commercial Housing Sales Contract signed with Yingtai Company, had the right to request Yingtai Company to deliver the purchased commercial housing as agreed. As an ordinary contractual creditor's right, this claim had no basis for priority protection. However, when CCB Huaihua City Branch paid the vast majority of the purchase price as agreed and actually possessed the purchased property, its ordinary creditor's right under the contract transformed into an expectant right of property in the property. Although this expectant right of property still falls within the category of creditor's rights, it is no longer the same as an ordinary creditor's right. As the seller, Yingtai Company transferred to the buyer, CCB Huaihua City Branch, the property rights of possession, use, benefit, and partial disposition over the sold property. CCB Huaihua City Branch also gained a certain degree of external publicity effect due to its actual possession of the property, although that effect is not yet equivalent to the statutory effect of real property registration. Accordingly, although the right enjoyed by CCB Huaihua City Branch over the property in question does not yet constitute a property right (ownership) within the meaning of the Civil Code of the PRC, it already possesses the substantive elements of a property right. CCB Huaihua City Branch could reasonably expect to convert this expectant right of property into a property right (ownership) within the meaning of the Civil Code of the PRC through registration of the real property. Moreover, the right arising from possession should also be protected under the possession regime of the Civil Code of the PRC. Therefore, this expectant right of property has a basis for priority protection over ordinary creditor's rights.

A mortgage right, on the other hand, is a type of security interest expressly provided for by the Civil Code of the PRC. Where the debtor fails to perform its matured debt, or circumstances agreed upon by the parties for realization of the mortgage right occur, the mortgagee has the right to seek priority satisfaction from the mortgaged property. In this case, Huarong Hunan Branch and Yingtai Company entered into a Mortgage Agreement, under which Yingtai Company provided the unsold commercial real estate under construction of Phase II of the Yingtai International Project (including the property in question) and the apportioned land as mortgage security for its debt owed to Huarong Hunan Branch, and the mortgage registration for construction in progress was completed. The mortgage right of Huarong Hunan Branch over the mortgaged property was lawfully established. The Hunan High People's Court Civil Judgment (2014) Xiang Gao Fa Min Er Chu Zi No. 32 also confirmed the priority right of satisfaction of Huarong Hunan Branch over the aforementioned mortgaged property. Accordingly, the mortgage right enjoyed by Huarong Hunan Branch has a legal basis for priority over ordinary creditor's rights in satisfaction.

2. In terms of the temporal order of obtaining the rights, Huarong Hunan Branch's mortgage right came first, and CCB Huaihua City Branch's expectant right of property came later.

Regarding the right enjoyed by CCB Huaihua City Branch over the property in question, based on the facts found, on January 31, 2013, Yingtai Company and CCB Huaihua City Branch entered into a Commercial Housing Sales Contract, agreeing that Yingtai Company would sell the property in question to CCB Huaihua City Branch at a total price of RMB 17,013,800, with taxes and fees of RMB 1,055,891. Before and after the signing of the contract, CCB Huaihua City Branch or CCB Hunan Branch remitted RMB 1,000,000, RMB 15,163,110, and RMB 500,000 respectively on December 31, 2009, March 28, 2013, and November 27, 2013, to the designated account of Yingtai Company. On November 18, 2013, CCB Huaihua City Branch and Huaihua Yingtai Shopping Center Management Co., Ltd. entered into the Yingtai International Property Management Contract. On December 2, 2013, CCB Huaihua City Branch paid RMB 23,679 in property management fees. Although CCB Huaihua City Branch claimed that, according to the Commercial Housing Sales Contract, the delivery time was before March 29, 2013, and that it paid the majority of the purchase price on March 28, 2013 and actually took delivery that day, CCB Huaihua City Branch did not submit any evidence of actual delivery at that time. The Yingtai International Property Delivery Procedure Form provided by Yingtai Company shows that the delivery procedures were processed on November 29, 2013. CCB Huaihua City Branch did not dispute the authenticity of this evidence, only arguing at trial that the date recorded on the delivery procedure form was inconsistent with the actual delivery date and also inconsistent with the date recorded on the Approval Form for Acceptance of Security Facilities Construction Projects in Financial Institution Business Premises. After trial, it submitted further opinions on the evidence, arguing that the form had defects and was not formal evidence of delivery. In fact, even based on the Approval Form for Acceptance of Security Facilities Construction Projects in Financial Institution Business Premises and the Approval Form for Acceptance of Security Facilities Construction Projects in Financial Institution Business Premises provided by CCB Huaihua City Branch, the project start date was August 28, 2013, and the acceptance date by the Huaihua City public security authorities was December 6, 2013. However, this approval form alone is insufficient to infer that CCB Huaihua City Branch actually possessed the property on the start date of the project, let alone to conclude that CCB Huaihua City Branch actually possessed the property on March 28, 2013. As for the Letter on Application for Installation of Three-Phase Electricity to the Premises submitted by Yingtai Company at second instance, which was issued by CCB Huaihua City Branch to Yingtai Company on May 10, 2013, even assuming its authenticity, its content is merely CCB Huaihua City Branch's application to Yingtai Company for installation of three-phase AC electricity and its commitment to bear the apportioned costs. Therefore, it is difficult to conclude from this that the property was actually delivered to CCB Huaihua City Branch at that time or earlier. Moreover, during the second instance trial, Yingtai Company stated that based on the Yingtai International Property Delivery Procedure Form, the delivery time signed by its sales department was November 29, 2013, and regarding whether there was an earlier delivery of the property to CCB Huaihua City Branch, Yingtai Company also submitted a written statement after trial, clearly stating that it could not verify. Considering the Yingtai International Property Delivery Procedure Form, the Yingtai International Property Management Contract, and other evidence and related facts, the time when Yingtai Company delivered the property to CCB Huaihua City Branch, and when CCB Huaihua City Branch actually possessed the property and obtained the expectant right of property over it, should be November 2013. This finding is consistent with the actual circumstances of the case.

As for Huarong Hunan Branch's mortgage right, based on the facts found, on May 23, 2013, Huarong Hunan Branch and Yingtai Company entered into the Mortgage Agreement, stipulating that Yingtai Company would provide the unsold commercial real estate under construction of Phase II of the Yingtai International Project (including the property in question) and the apportioned land as mortgage security for its debt owed to Huarong Hunan Branch. On May 27, 2013, Huarong Hunan Branch and Yingtai Company completed the mortgage registration for construction in progress with the Huaihua City Real Estate Administration Bureau, and the mortgage right of Huarong Hunan Branch over the above mortgaged property was lawfully established.

Accordingly, although the time of signing the contract by CCB Huaihua City Branch was earlier than that of Huarong Hunan Branch, its expectant right of property over the property in question was clearly later than Huarong Hunan Branch's lawfully established mortgage right.

3. In terms of fault in obtaining the rights, the existing evidence cannot prove that Huarong Hunan Branch was at fault in the process of establishing the mortgage, whereas CCB Huaihua City Branch failed to exercise due diligence in the process of purchasing the property and was to some extent negligent.

At second instance, Huarong Hunan Branch submitted the Legal Due Diligence Report on Commercial Acquisition and Restructuring Business issued by Hunan Rongcheng Law Firm on May 17, 2013, together with the Certificate of Inquiry Results of the Online Signing Information System of Huaihua City Real Estate Bureau submitted at first instance, to demonstrate that it had exercised due diligence in the process of establishing the mortgage, including that its entrusted intermediary had conducted on-site inspection of the property and inquired about the registration status at the real estate registration authority, and had not found that CCB Huaihua City Branch had contracted to purchase or actually possessed the property, or that the property had been mortgaged, or that any advance notice registration existed. CCB Huaihua City Branch did not recognize the authenticity, legality, or relevance of the Legal Due Diligence Report, and submitted the Supreme People's Court Civil Judgment (2021) Min Zhong No. 534 as new evidence at second instance. Relying on the finding in that case that Huarong Hunan Branch failed to exercise due diligence when establishing a mortgage over the property purchased by Dong Yurong, CCB Huaihua City Branch argued that Huarong Hunan Branch was also grossly negligent in this case. Upon examination, in the (2021) Min Zhong No. 534 case, Dong Yurong, as the buyer, signed and occupied the purchased property before Huarong Hunan Branch established the mortgage, which is clearly different from the facts in this case, where CCB Huaihua City Branch occupied the purchased property after Huarong Hunan Branch established the mortgage. In the (2021) Min Zhong No. 534 case, Dong Yurong provided the Yingtai International Property Delivery Procedure Form, Yingtai International Property Management Contract, Owner's Convention, Yingtai International Fire Safety Responsibility Agreement, and other evidence to show that Yingtai Company delivered the purchased property to Dong Yurong on May 9, 2013. In this case, however, the Yingtai International Property Delivery Procedure Form, Yingtai International Property Management Contract, and other evidence show that Yingtai Company delivered the property to CCB Huaihua City Branch in November 2013. Given that the developer, Yingtai Company, maliciously engaged in "selling first and then mortgaging," and that CCB Huaihua City Branch did not carry out online signing and filing or advance notice registration as required by regulations and the contract, and did not actually possess the purchased property, the failure of Huarong Hunan Branch to discover that the property had been sold when establishing the mortgage does not violate common sense. Accordingly, the existing evidence cannot prove that Huarong Hunan Branch failed to exercise due diligence in the process of establishing the mortgage. CCB Huaihua City Branch's claim that Huarong Hunan Branch was grossly negligent in this case lacks sufficient basis and cannot be sustained.

However, CCB Huaihua City Branch, as a specialized financial institution, generally has more complete contract management measures, stricter payment procedures, and higher internal risk prevention capabilities. In the process of purchasing the property, it should exercise a higher degree of diligence than ordinary buyers. In this case, Article 24 of the Commercial Housing Sales Contract signed on January 31, 2013, between Yingtai Company (seller) and CCB Huaihua City Branch (buyer) stipulated: "This contract shall take effect from the date of signing by both parties." Article 25 stipulated: "For pre-sale of commercial housing, within 30 days after this contract takes effect, the seller shall apply to the local real estate administration bureau for advance notice registration of the commercial housing." Although the contract placed the obligation to apply for advance notice registration on the seller Yingtai Company, since advance notice registration directly concerns the buyer's substantive rights in the purchased property, CCB Huaihua City Branch, as the buyer, should have taken proactive steps, such as urging Yingtai Company or suspending payment of the purchase price, to compel Yingtai Company to apply for advance notice registration as agreed when Yingtai Company failed to do so within 30 days after the contract took effect. Former Article 20(1) of the Property Law of the PRC provided: "Where the parties enter into an agreement for the sale of a house or any other immovable property, they may, for the purpose of ensuring the realization of the property right in the future, apply to the registration authority for advance notice registration in accordance with the agreement. After the advance notice registration, any disposal of the immovable property without the consent of the holder of the advance notice registration right shall not have the effect of property right." Accordingly, if advance notice registration had been completed for the property in question, it would have been protected under property law, creating the legal effect of notifying an indefinite number of persons that the property had been purchased by CCB Huaihua City Branch, and thereby preventing Yingtai Company from maliciously engaging in irregular practices such as "one property sold twice" or "selling first and then mortgaging," and the rights of CCB Huaihua City Branch as a buyer would have been effectively safeguarded. However, in reality, the existing evidence shows that even though Yingtai Company failed to apply for advance notice registration within the required period (within 30 days from January 31, 2013), CCB Huaihua City Branch not only failed to urge Yingtai Company to fulfill the advance notice registration obligation but also, through CCB Hunan Branch, paid the majority of the purchase price (RMB 15,163,110) to Yingtai Company on March 28, 2013, which clearly indicates a disregard for its own rights and demonstrates that CCB Huaihua City Branch did not give sufficient attention to possible changes in ownership or increases in encumbrances over the property it purchased. This provided an opportunity for Yingtai Company to engage in the irregular practice of "selling first and then mortgaging," leading to a conflict of rights between CCB Huaihua City Branch, as the earlier buyer, and Huarong Hunan Branch, as the later mortgagee. CCB Huaihua City Branch was to some extent negligent in this regard. CCB Huaihua City Branch's argument that it was not at fault at all regarding the failure to transfer or apply for advance notice registration of the property cannot be sustained, and this court does not support it.

4. From the perspective of reducing or preventing recurrence of risks, the risk liability of the parties to the prior and subsequent transactions should be allocated fairly.

In practice, dishonest developers often take advantage of information asymmetry and their dominant position in a seller's market to engage in irregular practices such as "one property sold twice" or "selling first and then mortgaging," harming the lawful rights of prior buyers and defrauding subsequent buyers or mortgagees, leading to numerous conflicts of rights and resulting disputes and litigation. This not only consumes judicial resources and increases the burden on litigants but also erodes social integrity and affects social stability. To minimize or prevent the risk of such conflicts and disputes, in addition to holding the developer, which has seriously breached good faith, liable in accordance with laws and regulations, financial institutions, in the process of accepting mortgages, should also strictly examine in accordance with laws and regulations, conduct prudent, comprehensive, and good-faith investigations into the status of the mortgaged property, to reduce or prevent the risk of the developer's dishonesty or malicious harm to prior buyers' rights, and also to avoid becoming involved in unnecessary disputes and litigation, thereby ensuring the safety of credit funds or related claims, and further maintaining the healthy and stable development of the socialist market economic order. If the mortgagee fails to examine in accordance with laws and regulations, fails to exercise necessary due diligence, and accepts the mortgage when it knew or should have known that the property used by the debtor for mortgage had already been sold to others, leading to a conflict of rights and resulting disputes and litigation with the prior buyer, then it may bear the corresponding adverse consequences and assume the corresponding risks. On the other hand, buyers, especially specialized financial institutions like CCB Huaihua City Branch, should, when purchasing property, carefully assess the developer's qualifications, financial standing, and reputation, and during the signing and payment process, actively protect their rights through lawful means such as online signing and filing, advance notice registration, urging for transfer, and suspending payment, to avoid the purchased property being in a state of uncertain title due to lack of publicity or registration, thereby providing opportunities for dishonest developers to engage in irregular practices such as "one property sold twice" or "selling first and then mortgaging," and exposing their own property rights to the risk of enforcement by other claimants and the inability to transfer registration. If the buyer fails to fulfill statutory or contractual obligations, or disregards its own rights, and takes no measures despite being fully capable of taking necessary actions without significantly increasing performance costs that would avoid conflicts with third-party rights and prevent its own losses, then it may bear the corresponding adverse consequences and assume the corresponding risks. In this case, as discussed above, CCB Huaihua City Branch, as the prior buyer, disregarded its own rights when Yingtai Company failed to apply for advance notice registration for the property as agreed, and failed to take relevant measures. It bears some negligence for the occurrence of the conflict of rights and the litigation. Causing CCB Huaihua City Branch to bear the adverse consequences and assume the corresponding risks in this case is conducive to reducing or preventing the recurrence of such risks, reducing unnecessary litigation burdens for relevant actors, and is also consistent with the principle of fairness and the actual circumstances of this case. In its future business operations, CCB Huaihua City Branch should enhance its awareness of contracts, rights, and risks, strengthen internal control management of contract signing, payment procedures, etc., and try to avoid unnecessary conflicts with others' rights that could cause its own losses.

Based on the above analysis, Huarong Hunan Branch has a mortgage right over the property in question, and CCB Huaihua City Branch has an expectant right of property over the property in question, both of which have priority over ordinary creditor's rights. The signing of the contract by CCB Huaihua City Branch occurred first, but the time when it obtained the expectant right of property over the property was later than the time when Huarong Hunan Branch obtained its mortgage right. The existing evidence cannot prove that Huarong Hunan Branch was at fault in the process of establishing the mortgage, whereas CCB Huaihua City Branch failed to take active measures in response to Yingtai Company's breach of contract and bears some negligence for the occurrence of the conflict of rights and the litigation. In this case, causing CCB Huaihua City Branch to bear the adverse consequences is conducive to reducing or preventing the recurrence of such disputes. Therefore, the mortgage right of Huarong Hunan Branch over the property in question should take priority over the expectant right of property of CCB Huaihua City Branch. The first instance judgment, which did not support CCB Huaihua City Branch's objection and dismissed its claims, was not erroneous, and this court affirms it.

As for the Supreme People's Court Civil Judgment (2021) Min Zhong No. 534, although it applied Article 28 of the Provisions on Enforcement Objection and Review by reference, it also made a substantive comparison of the rights of Dong Yurong and Huarong Hunan Branch over the property in question, finding that Dong Yurong purchased and possessed the property first, Huarong Hunan Branch established the mortgage later, and Huarong Hunan Branch, when establishing the mortgage over the property that Dong Yurong had purchased and actually occupied, failed to exercise due diligence and was at fault. Therefore, Dong Yurong's expectant right of property over the property was entitled to priority protection. As discussed above, the basic facts of this case differ significantly from those in the (2021) Min Zhong No. 534 case. CCB Huaihua City Branch's claim that, under the principle of like cases being treated alike, this case should follow the (2021) Min Zhong No. 534 Civil Judgment and support CCB Huaihua City Branch's claim for exclusion of enforcement is not supported by this court.

In conclusion, the appeal of CCB Huaihua City Branch cannot be sustained and should be dismissed. The first instance judgment found the facts essentially clearly, and although there were flaws in the application of law, the result was correct. This court affirms it. Pursuant to Article 177(1)(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC and Article 332 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the judgment is as follows:

Appeal dismissed, and the original judgment affirmed.
